steps.action: Pose the unsolved question of which boundary conditions, stretching/shortening rate ratios, crustal strengths and inheritance allow coeval normal, thrust and strike-slip regimes, noting the lack of systematic study.

end.claim: In scaled crustal analog models with simultaneous shortening and orthogonal stretching, normal, thrust and strike-slip faults coexist in brittle crust only for intermediate-to-high Ve/Vs (about 1.4 and above, with thrusting inhibited at Ve/Vs ≥ 2 for low shortening), not in brittle-ductile crust; strike-slip orientation depends on strength and inheritance; and prior normal faults are reactivated, never inverted, under fault-parallel shortening.

decisive_move.sentence: Independent step-motor control of stretching and shortening velocities, setting Ve/Vs from 0 to 2.8 under non-plane-strain conditions, is what makes the regime-coexistence regularities possible.

gates.evidence: No hypothesis is stated before the experiments; the design varies Ve/Vs, layering and inheritance to explore (§2.3 ¶3, §3.1.1 ¶1). The claims face only comparisons with Andersonian and Coulomb expectations (§4.1 ¶1, §4.2 ¶1), which partly fail (anomalous 60-70° strike-slip faults), and qualitative comparison with nature (§4.5). Nothing is reported as fixed before the data.

limits: Each boundary condition is run once; no reproduction runs are reported, so run-to-run variability is unknown. The Ve/Vs threshold for coexisting regimes is stated inconsistently: 1.4 < Ve/Vs < 2 (§0 ¶1), > 1.4 (§4.1 ¶3), ≥ 1.4 (§4.5 ¶1, §5 ¶4), > 1 (§5 ¶2), and Ve/Vs > 0.9 as the minimum for lateral escape (§4.5 ¶2). Models reach different strain amounts (BI07 3.6 %, BI11 2.2 % shortening), and the authors concede thrusts might appear later (§4.1 ¶3, §4.1 ¶4), so the thresholds hold only within the imposed strain (<20 %, foam limit, §2.1 ¶2). The supplement (Figs. S1-S3) was not supplied; steps citing it are coded from main-text descriptions. No review file or open discussion was supplied, although the paper went through Solid Earth discussion with two referees, so no review sequence is coded. Sub-claims at other statuses: the brittle-thickness explanation of strength control (§4.3 ¶1) and inherited-structure control of strike-slip orientation (§4.2 ¶3) are best_explanation, with boundary effects not excluded; compatibility with natural cases (§4.5 ¶4, §4.5 ¶5) is qualitative analogy, at most best_explanation; the explanation for absent inversion (§4.5 ¶5) is unresolved among stated rivals. Composition is coded exploration_first by inference: conditions are varied systematically and rivals appear only post hoc. A general question precedes the experiments, so the fit is imperfect. The density-ratio buoyancy effect in CE models is argued to be minor but not tested (§2.2 ¶2).

disagreements.target: Basin inversion analog models of Del Ventisette et al. (2006), Sani et al. (2007) and Deng et al. (2020)
disagreements.support: Their basin-parallel shortening produced inversion, while none of the present two-stage models inverted; the authors attribute the difference to coeval orthogonal extension and internal parameters, with BI01 as partial evidence.
disagreements.quote: These results differ from previous basin inversion analog models by

disagreements.target: Brittle analog models of strike-slip systems during compression (Duarte et al., 2011; Rosas et al., 2012, 2015)
disagreements.support: Confined walls and a prescribed mobile discontinuity in those setups prevented typical V-shaped strike-slip systems, which the present unconstrained setup produces.
disagreements.quote: strike-slip fault strike and activity were constrained by the chosen setup

disagreements.target: Previous inversion modeling studies (e.g., McClay 1995; Bonini et al. 2012; Zwaan et al. 2022)
disagreements.support: Those studies apply parallel or low-angle stretching and contraction, whereas nature (San Jorge basin) shows fault-parallel contraction, which the present models test.
disagreements.quote: In general, the applied directions of stretching and successive contraction are parallel (in 2D numerical or analog models) or oblique but at low angles.

disagreements.target: Mantle-scale brittle-ductile indentation analog experiments (e.g., Davy and Cobbold 1988; Ratschbacher et al. 1991; Martinod et al. 2000)
disagreements.support: Those models simulate larger domains and do not kinematically control lateral escape, limiting direct comparison.
disagreements.quote: However, a direct comparison with our models is difficult

disagreements.target: Use of fault-type associations as indicators of relative shortening and stretching rates
disagreements.support: Models with the same boundary conditions but different inheritance or strength produce different fault associations.
disagreements.quote: the association of specific types of faults cannot be used as an indicator of the relative rate of shortening and stretching
